title: What’s new with Microsoft in open-source and Kubernetes at KubeCon North America 2026
summary: Explore new Kubernetes and open-source innovations from Microsoft across AKS, AI infrastructure, fleets, security, and upgrades.
body_markdown:
Kubernetes works best when you tell it what you want running and let controllers keep at it until the cluster matches. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, most of what we’re extending is that model to work that has traditionally lived outside this declarative style of management.


That work often ends up in scripts, runbooks, or with someone watching a dashboard. Device plugins let Kubernetes count GPUs but not describe them. Across a fleet, it’s hard to know which clusters have drifted, and the call on whether to continue an upgrade often comes down to whoever is watching. Agents add their own needs: runs that can pause and pick up again later, strong isolation for the code they execute, and no dependency on one framework or cloud.


Since[my last update](https://opensource.microsoft.com/blog/2026/03/24/whats-new-with-microsoft-in-open-source-and-kubernetes-at-kubecon-cloudnativecon-europe-2026/) at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2026, much of our work upstream and in Microsoft Azure has gone into these problems.


[Explore Azure Kubernetes Service](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/kubernetes-service/)


## Building in the open


This cycle’s upstream work spans secure workload isolation, portable agent infrastructure, inference, and capacity across sites:


- [Hyperlight](https://github.com/hyperlight-dev/hyperlight) , a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox project, provides lightweight, hypervisor-backed isolation for cloud-native workloads. Its integration with the Linux Foundation’s Unikraft project brought support for[.NET, Python, Node.js, PowerShell, and more](https://github.com/hyperlight-dev/hyperlight-unikraft/tree/main/examples) , while extended[urunc](https://urunc.io/hypervisor-support/) support brings that isolation to another CNCF runtime.
- We’re also exploring[Lampyr](https://github.com/hyperlight-dev/lampyr) , an early-stage effort to extend these isolation capabilities to serverless computing and lightweight Kubernetes workloads. For developers, that means secure execution with less overhead, developed in the open where you can help shape it.
- [Agent Substrate](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate) provides portable, secure infrastructure for running across clouds. Microsoft engineers are contributing to various streams, including pluggable snapshot storage, Kubernetes identity support, micro virtual machine (microVM) runtime reliability, and worker lifecycle management.
- We are also building vendor-neutral pieces on top of that agent infrastructure:[sessions](https://github.com/agent-primitives/sessions) gives an agent run a durable, replayable lifecycle across runtimes, while[suite](https://github.com/agent-primitives/suite) handles portable agent packaging. Agents can then suspend, resume, replay, or branch on Kubernetes, so developers can build workflows that survive interruptions without rebuilding lifecycle management for each framework, runtime, or cloud.
- [AI Runway](https://github.com/ai-runway/airunway) has been accepted as a CNCF Sandbox project. It gives Kubernetes a native way to deploy and manage inference across multiple providers, so teams can try different combinations of open source inference engines and models without leaving the workflows they already use.
- [Unbounded](https://unbounded-cloud.io/) , which is in the queue to join the CNCF Sandbox, extends any conformant Kubernetes control plane with worker nodes in other clouds, on-premises, on bare metal, and at the edge, with provisioning and cross-site networking built in. Because it builds on standard Kubernetes APIs, platform teams can reach distributed capacity from the control plane they already have, without adopting a proprietary orchestration model.


### New leadership roles


Open source communities also depend on people willing to step up and lead, and I’m proud of the Microsoft engineers who did this year across the CNCF:


- Lachie Evenson—Vice Chair of the CNCF Governing Board.
- Jack Francis—chair of the Kubernetes Autoscaling special interest group (SIG).
- Heba Elayoty—chair of Kubernetes SIG Scheduling.
- Jon Huhn—Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) code reviewer.
- Jackie Maertens—Istio maintainer.
- Hariharan Subramanian—Envoy Gateway reviewer.


## What’s new in Azure Kubernetes Service


In addition to our upstream work, I’m happy to share new capabilities in[Azure Kubernetes Service](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/kubernetes-service/) (AKS) and[Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/kubernetes-fleet-manager) across AI infrastructure, multi-cluster operations, upgrades, and security.


### AI infrastructure on upstream Kubernetes APIs


AI and HPC workloads often need specific kinds of GPUs and networking, but device plugins only let them ask for a number of devices. Teams running remote direct memory access (RDMA) over InfiniBand also have managed drivers and device plugins. With this release, those teams can schedule GPUs and high-performance networking through upstream Kubernetes APIs, and AKS runs the drivers.


Dynamic resource allocation (DRA) replaces fixed device counts with a model where a workload describes the hardware it needs and Kubernetes assigns a match. AKS now offers[managed support for DRANET](https://aka.ms/aks/managed-support-for-dranet) , the DRA-network driver maintained in Kubernetes-sigs, on RDMA-capable node pools for distributed training and HPC jobs, and[managed DRA for GPU node pools](https://aka.ms/aks/managed-dra-for-gpus) brings the same model to GPUs. DRANET also powers[multiple network interface card (multi-NIC) support](https://aka.ms/aks/multi-nic) , which attaches dedicated interfaces on separate subnets directly to pods.


### Simpler multi-cluster operations


Fleet placement works like the rest of Kubernetes; the hub holds the desired state, and member clusters are kept in line with it. In practice, people edit member clusters directly, new clusters join with workloads already running, and resources sometimes have to come off a cluster without disrupting the applications that use them.


Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager, built on the CNCF Sandbox project KubeFleet, gives platform teams a single control plane for placing Kubernetes resources across clusters. Lessons from[COSMIC](https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/27363-microsoft-azure-kubernetes-service) , the internal platform Microsoft 365 engineering teams run on AKS, have helped shape Fleet and how we think about running clusters at scale.


Three placement controls for those situations are now generally available:


1. [Drift detection](https://aka.ms/kubernetes-fleet/placement/drift-detection) flags resources that no longer match their placement configuration.
2. [Takeover](https://aka.ms/kubernetes-fleet/placement/takeover) lets Fleet Manager adopt workloads on a joining cluster under rules the platform team sets.
3. [Eviction](https://aka.ms/kubernetes-fleet/placement/eviction-disruption-budget) removes resources from a member cluster without connecting to it, and a disruption budget caps how many placements go offline at once.


For simpler cases,[annotation-based placement](https://aka.ms/kubernetes-fleet/placement/annotations) declares target clusters with annotations on a standard Kubernetes resource instead of a separate placement object.


### Safer upgrades


Upgrade blockers often surface only after an upgrade has started, and stopping a bad one usually depends on someone watching dashboards. Two new capabilities address both:


- [Upgrade insights](https://aka.ms/aks-upgrade-insights) checks readiness before a cluster or node image upgrade begins and flags issues like restrictive pod disruption budgets, deprecated APIs, and quota or subnet limits, with remediation guidance for individual clusters and for the fleet.
- [Upgrade health gates](https://aka.ms/aks-upgrade-health-gates) evaluates node, cluster, and workload health, including signals from your own monitoring tools, and stops the upgrade from progressing when health deteriorates. The judgment call that used to belong to whoever was watching becomes a check that runs every time.


### Security and network visibility


Security teams need to know that code on their nodes, including inside container images, comes from trusted sources and hasn’t been altered.[Azure Container Linux](https://aka.ms/azurecontainerlinux) , the immutable, container-optimized host operating system for AKS, now supports Integrity Policy Enforcement (IPE), generally available in audit mode.


IPE is a Linux security module, merged upstream in kernel 6.12, that validates executable code against signed dm-verity volumes. In audit mode it logs untrusted or tampered code without blocking it, so teams can fix problems before turning on enforcement. Node auto-provisioning[now supports Azure Container Linux too](https://aka.ms/nap) , so nodes provisioned on demand for pending pods run on the same hardened host.


Flow-log aggregation in container network observability keeps storage costs predictable, but it drops the fields that security and connectivity investigations rely on. With[configurable dimensions for container network observability](https://aka.ms/acns/howtoenablecnl) , teams choose which fields aggregation keeps, such as domain names, per-pod IP addresses, and HTTP URLs, and filter logs and metrics by Cilium identity.


The thread running through all of this is the one we started with. Kubernetes is at its best when the system, rather than a person, keeps what’s running matched to what you asked for. Each time a decision moves out of a runbook and into a controller, platform teams get some of their attention back. GPUs, fleets, upgrades, and agents are where that’s happening next, and most of the work is in the open where you can shape it.


## Get involved


Stay connected with the AKS community, explore the latest developments, and share your feedback. Here are a few ways to get involved:


- Track what’s planned, in progress, and shipped on the[AKS public roadmap](https://github.com/orgs/Azure/projects/685) , and open an issue or feature request in the[AKS GitHub repo](https://github.com/Azure/AKS) .
- Join the[AKS Community Calls](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLc3Ep462vVYu0eMSiORonzj3utqYu285z) for roadmap updates and Q&A with the product team, and subscribe to the[AKS YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@theakscommunity) for technical walkthroughs.
- Check the[AKS release notes](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/releases) to see when features move from preview to general availability.
- Try, file issues on, or contribute to the upstream projects in this post, including[Hyperlight](https://github.com/hyperlight-dev/hyperlight) ,[Agent Substrate](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate) ,[AI Runway](https://github.com/ai-runway/airunway) , and[Unbounded](https://unbounded-cloud.io/) .
